You need to cut those first two lines, move the third line up to the top so your topic introduction can happen in the first 1 to 2 seconds. I often refer to this concept as speed to value. Your hit rate for comprehension goes up and then confusion goes down. Now, the tactics for how to improve clarity is really about becoming a better writer. You want to use fewer words, but enough that the viewer can't misunderstand you. You want to use simpler words, ideally at a sixth grade reading level. So, you've eliminated delay and you've maximized the clarity, getting rid of the confusion so the viewer knows exactly what the video is going to be about. Problem number three, irrelevance means that the viewer is not confident that what's coming next in the video after the hook is going to be valuable enough to help them solve a problem. So, they know what the video is about, but they're unclear if it's relevant for them. Now, there are two easy ways to solve this problem. The first way is to say the word you or your instead of the words me or I when you're delivering the hook. Most people think you should make hooks like this. I've struggled with skin problems my whole life. The problem is this opens a door in the viewer's mind to question if they see themselves in the creator because they're thinking this, well, if you struggle with these problems, do I also struggle with the same problems you do? That's what they're questioning in their mind. If the viewer doesn't see themsel in the creator for a number of different reasons, they're going to put less value in the incoming solution, and they'll stop watching. This is the irrelevance problem. The viewer doesn't feel like what's coming next will be relevant for them. So, to solve this problem, all you have to do is frame your hooks using you and your. So instead of saying, "I've struggled with skin problems my whole life," you say, "If you've struggled with skin problems your whole life," dot dot dot. When you do this, the viewer feels like the video is targeted for them. There's no possible question or misunderstanding because you're saying it's for you for your problems. And this makes the viewer hold on longer for the hook. Now, the second way to solve for the relevance problem is to frame your hooks around expected value. There are two types of videos: entertainment and education. Both of these offer solutions to a painoint. That solution is value. Entertainment offers a solve for boredom. Education offers a solve for a specific problem. If you want your hook to feel more relevant for your viewer, all you have to do is agitate a painoint that they already have so that you can tee up a solution that is for them. For example, can you tell the difference between these two hooks? The first one is these are three common trends in skincare. And the second one is if you struggle with acne, try these three things. Learning about trends in skincare is a nice to have. Solving my acne problem is a need to have. So, if you frame the hook around a known painoint and you deliver it using you and your instead of me and my, the video will seem more targeted for the viewer and it will hook them more. Okay, the last hook problem number four is disinterest. And this is the one that most people fixate on the most. At this point, the viewer is clear on the topic, believes there is some relevance or value incoming for them, but the hook still just doesn't grab them enough. This is the curiosity problem. The hook just doesn't make the viewer curious enough to want to keep watching. So, what you want to do in the hook to solve the disinterest problem is build a curiosity loop. And everybody talks about curiosity loop, but nobody ever explains what it is. A curiosity loop is when the viewer sees something, asks a hypothetical question in their mind, gets some additional context to answer it, but that spurs a new question, more context, new question, more context, and so on. They keep opening loops throughout the entire video. That's what a curiosity loop really is. So, your job in the hook is to open that initial curiosity loop and start the spiral. What is that initial question that the viewer has where they can't look away? They just have to wait for more context to answer it. So, the $10 million content question really is this. How do you always drive curiosity and build that curiosity loop every single time, no matter what type of video you're making? And the way you do this is by setting up contrast or comparison in the hook. Contrast is simply the distance between the current common belief of the viewer and some contrarian or alternative perspective that you offer. So, for example, if I say in the hook, this one trick will clear up all your acne in 45 minutes without any side effects. What I'm really doing is creating a comparison in your mind to the current baseline. You got to wait 6 months, take Accutane, go through all these side effects versus my contrarian offer, 45 minutes, no side effects, quick solve. That distance is contrast. What happens when you do this in the viewer subconscious is that when you frame a comparison, A something they know and B something they don't, B triggers the sticky pain point they have from A not solving their pain. And so essentially that comparison acts as a reagitator of that painoint which gets them curious because they want to solve it. To simplify all this, if you're not following what I'm saying, it's A versus B. A is what they already believe. B is some alternative that you're suggesting that makes their pain point solved faster, better, or cheaper. Now, getting good at learning how to create this contrast with words is really the secret to driving curiosity whenever you want. It's honestly the secret to storytelling at a macro level. Now, I'm not going to go too deep into exactly how to build this contrast and curiosity because it really does differ for every scenario. But what I will say is this, there are two types of contrast. Implied contrast and stated contrast. Stated contrast is when you share verbally both A and B explicitly. So, for example, saying something like this, "Most people solve their acne with Accutane, but I have an herbal remedy that does it three times faster." You're stating Accutane verse herbal remedy, so it's impossible to miss what that contrast is. The other type of contrast, which is way more subtle, is implied. And in this case, you say what the contrarian alternative is, but you don't reference the base because it's implied. People know what the base solution is. So for example, if I say if you want to solve your acne, this herbal supplement is eight times more effective. If the common viewer already knows what the baseline solutions are, nothing, Accutane, whatever they are, then you don't need to say it again because it's implied what their baseline understanding is. Essentially, it's your contrarian take versus the field of all other options. So you really have two options to create the contrast. You can go stated, which is way more blunt, A versus B, impossible to misunderstand, or you can go implied, which is a little bit more savvy and you don't really call it out specifically. Now, tactically, when you're writing hooks, typically the topic clarity comes in the first sentence, and then you set up that contrast in the following one to two sentences. This is why I consider hooks to really be like two to three lines. They're not always just a single punchy line. Sometimes you can achieve the clarity and the contrast all together in one line. And if you can, those are the easiest hooks that you can reuse.   16. @mattyjwalks: Since the circa 1960s, there were no actual "restrictions" that barred films from an unnatural look. In the early days, a scanner would display a positive image from a film negative where a user could use varying intensity of red, green, and blue printer lights to create an overall cast on the film, while  exposure and contrast would have already been determined by both on-set lighting and whether the film was pushed or pulled during the later development process . By the 1970s, film prints could be made using perviously developed negative, yet allowing per-RGB channel Lift, Gain, and Gamma adjustments to be made alongside the traditional RGB printer light method including digital scopes, resulting in an analog workflow that matched todays grading standards. So, color grades now are a sign of the times just as the 'neutral' look of older films was before. I must admit, however, that the industry has gotten better at color grading with digital tools since the 2010s.

  18. @dutu000: I really hate the way most modern movies look. The color palette looks "poor". They are actually "poor in colors". And I think this is because of the color grading abuse, combined with laziness on set and smaller budgets. For example... Say you want a teal and orange look. What do they do now? They shoot "normally", then, in post, play with the hues, throwing away colors, making everything either teal or orange. If you were to do this look on film, with no digital grading, you would have to paint the actual set tealish, choose costumes accordingly, pay attention to every little object in your scene. And, of course, light according to the filmstock (daylight/tungsten). I mean "correct white balance". And that teal and orange will look WAY richer than the one made digitally after the shooting. Because you are not taking colors away, compressing them to a certain hue. You will always get a glimpse of a non teal-orange color, also making the look "believable", as you said in the video. I think this is the main reason of this poor, "digital" look of the movies today. It's not that they are not shot on film... it's this approach. Why not shoot on digital, do tests and emulate a film stock in post, make a LUT, have that LUT in all monitors on the set, and construct the look of the film traditionally, on the set, by actually painting the set and choosing the colors of the costumes and props accordingly? I think that would make a ton of difference!

And almost every single round of initial video creative, we always make sure we have one of these POV ads in there essentially. And now pairing that with the word hate is also really smart because that is a really really powerful trigger word. But even a simple I hate XYZ has worked really well for a number of brands that I work with too. Which brings me to our next few hooks. These are actually going to be the best hooks that I've seen with both partnership ads as well as founders ads content because this is the type of content that I really see moving the needle across the board across all industries. Essentially, both of these strategies are must tests in the ad account, which is why I wanted to include them specifically. So, for founders content, I would make sure that you are always testing your round of founders content with these few hooks. Number one, explain why you built this company from the get. Again, this is very often going to show the multiple failed attempts that someone went through to eventually realize that they themselves needed to create this product, which is probably going to mimic a lot of your customer's journey. Another one is kind of controversial. I actually highly recommend that you always include a hook that has the founder introducing themselves and that they are the founder of the brand. This is one that actually I've heard a lot of marketing gurus say that you need to avoid because no one cares. But every time I end up testing this one, it often will become a top performer because again, I feel like initially it doesn't feel like an ad. It feels a lot more like that organic founder style content. And I've noticed especially in the US, we really champion entrepreneurs. They are like rock stars to us in many ways. Which is why when we see someone else on this entrepreneurial journey, we tend to listen in, especially if they're someone that is aspirational to us or someone who reminds us a little bit of ourselves. Another thing I'll say too is make sure that you have the name and that they're the founder in text overlay. This is something I've actually split test a lot and I find that it almost always outperforms not having it. Now, I do have an entire video that breaks down exactly how you can approach founders ads content even if you're not super comfortable on camera. And next up, partnership ads. And the great thing is too is that you can do partnership ads for free. You can run it with your founders content. You can make your own publications. There are many different ways for you to utilize partnership ads, but it is imperative that you do so. However, if you want to start investing in creator content, which ultimately should be your goal in the long term, these are the type of hooks that I see work really, really well. And the first one is actually inaction hooks. So, if you're working with a creator, be sure to put them in the action of their everyday. So, have them doing an activity, have them getting in the car. What I've really noticed is that it doesn't signal an ad if you have them making similar to their organic style content. And this is a really great way to have your product or service fit in a little bit more seamlessly to their everyday, which will make it a much better partnership than them just doing an ad read. And number eight is the emotional hook. I was going to try and cry for this one, but I just I just don't have it in me. I'm sorry. So things like people are mad at me because or why did I start crying when these are actually really big trends that I saw on organic social that have translated really well to creative that converts on meta. And hook number nine is the why did no one tell me hook. Here is the breakdown of this Ad


Mass Market Desire

it’s all about that core desire to look good, like wanting to ‘melt my FUPA.’ It’s tapping into that universal feeling of wanting to feel confident and happy with your body again.


Awareness Levels:

Strongest Appeal (Solution Aware):

This one’s for women who already know their struggle, menopause weight or that stubborn FUPA, and have tried stuff like supplements. 

The ad points out how frustrating it is to drop $874 on supplements that don’t work, then teases ‘THIS’ as the new, actually effective solution.

Problem Aware:

It calls out the pain points straight up, ‘Menopause’ and ‘FUPA’. and uses that big number ($874) to really hit home how annoying and urgent the problem is.


Sophistication Level:

Not Level 2: Goes beyond simple promises. it builds emotional tension with wasted money and failed attempts.

Closer to Level 3:

Audience is skeptical and jaded.

The hook contrasts failed “old mechanism” (supplements) with an implied new mechanism (the mysterious “THIS”).

This reframing positions the ad as a fresh, superior solution that cuts through doubt.

Persona:

this ad is talking to women dealing with menopause weight (like FUPA).

- The Psychology Behind Good Advertising: Kind: captions Language: en It should come as no surprise that modern advertising as we know it, has shaped our society in many ways. A lot of our daily decisions and life choices are influenced in part by advertising itself. It’s become such a deep-rooted constituent of our established norm that a world without it would seem, frankly, strange "Like so many others, I had become a slave to the IKEA nesting instinct" "Uh, yes. I'd like to order the Erica Pekkary dust ruffles" "Please hold." This is because barely a moment goes by during our day when we aren’t bombarded with advertisements in some form or the other. Posters, billboards, flyers, TV commercials, and internet ads, all creep into our personal space and tell us what we should buy and who we should be. For now our only brief escape from our role as a potential consumer comes to us during sleep. But even this could possibly change one day. "Are you bored?" "Get Sky Go for your mobile" "Best entertainment and live sport" "When you want it and where you want it" What's important to know is that the purpose of advertising isn’t limited in its capacity to harass us into parting with our hard earned money. Advertising plays a traditional role in helping businesses reach prospective customers and vice versa. Without it we would not know where to look for a particular product or service we need. Perhaps without advertising we wouldn’t even know what we wanted in the first place. Yet in our present day technologically driven lives, the reach between producer and consumer has grown a lot smaller. With the numerous media platforms and channels available to us, a simple online search takes us to a list of providers able to satisfy our every want. Our dilemma today comes in the form of not knowing which product to choose from out of the many available to us. This is where good advertising comes into play. In a saturated market, subtle differences can make the distinction between the choice of one product over another. There are typically two modes of advertising that ad agencies and marketing gurus utilize. One focuses on the qualities of the product, while the other seeks to arouse an emotional response from the intended audience. The moment you start to think about advertisements that have stood out to you in the recent past, there’s a high probability that they incorporated the latter. And there’s a good reason for this. "Well gentlemen, I don't think I have to tell you what you just witnessed here" "I think you do" Why should you choose one product over another? That decision becomes easy when you develop an affinity with a particular brand. It could be something as small as an aesthetically appealing logo design. Something that resonates with you and feels calming. The right colours and appropriate typography all matched in harmony for a well packaged product. But advertising goes beyond a well thought out logo or attractive packaging. The most successful ad campaigns hardly say anything about the product itself but instead create a lucid atmosphere that evokes a strong emotion from its target consumer. These are the types of advertisements that we remember, talk about, and influence our purchasing decisions. Now, let’s take a look at the following two commercials about perfume: "Fragrances by Shulton" "The essence of precious scents caught in that precise moment of fulfillment" "Distilled with exquisite artistry for your every mood" "In four fragrances" "Here's the newest adventure in fragrances" "Escapade" "A blending of subtle French genius with a bold, vivacious, American touch" "To be lovely is to feel lovely when your fragrance expresses your gayest self" "So choose a gay adventure - choose Escapade toilet water" "Immediately, you'll feel lovely" "Why, you are lovely in that light and gay Escapade mood" "And remember your Escapade stick cologne to a new adventure, wherever you are" "Enjoy all these fragrances" "Friendship's garden" "Early American Old Spice" "Dessert Flower - At leading cosmetic counters everywhere" "Toilet Waters at a $1.25 and a $1.50, stick colognes $1" "Acqua di Gioia, the new eau fraiche" "Giorgio Armani" The differences between the two commercials are quite stark. The first ad for Escapade Perfume quite explicitly focuses on the product itself. They describe certain characteristics of the perfume while going on to talk about its application and effect on the user. And this is quite difficult to do when describing a product whose main selling attribute (smell) is not transmissible through Television. It almost seems absurd, but the second perfume commercial for Giorgio Armani does not even try in the least to directly communicate the features of their product. They rely solely on alighting particular feelings and associations with their perfume. In this case, we could assume that the directors behind the ad wanted to transmit the feeling of ethereal beauty. We see a woman who fits into our standard of high attractiveness in our society, frolicking through a rainforest in the midst of a storm. The only mention of the perfume is in the last six seconds of the one minute ad. So why do we care about the associations of a product, rather than the product itself? Good advertising helps us begin to answer one of the most fundamental questions of life – Who Am I? This is because when it comes to figuring out who we are and what we want from life, we usually struggle to find answers. A lot of this is existential and has to do with the fact that we’re born with no pre-established notion of what it means to be human. It’s up to us to figure that along the way. But making that decision isn’t easy. In fact, it’s a huge burden. Out of all the possibilities our lives can take, how can we decide who or what we should be? We have no inkling if the choices we make will turn out to be good or not. Yet, we are each tasked with the responsibility of deciding for ourselves and can only hope that we’ve chosen well. On the other hand, good advertising helps us build an identity by releasing the anxiety brought about by self-determination. It tells us exactly what choice to make by compelling us to buy a certain product. And once we have done so, we will be able to emulate the identity and characteristics that we have learned to associate with that product from a particular commercial or advertisement. "Advertising is based on one thing" "Happiness" "And do you know what happiness is? Happiness is the smell of a new car" "It's freedom from fear. It's a billboard on the side of the road that screams, with reassurance, that whatever you're doing, it's okay." "You are okay" Advertising that caters to our feelings, primarily resonates with our subconscious mind and not our conscious mind. It’s why we sometimes can’t rationally deduce our preference for a certain brand and our ability to pay a premium for a product we can’t tell apart from its competitors. If we are drawn to it simply because of what it evokes inside of us and the associations that come with it, then rest assured, the marketing department has done their research. What this means is that we need to start thinking carefully about the decisions we make even if it’s something as insignificant as purchasing a perfume. Good advertising feeds off both our insecurities and deficiencies as humans and makes us believe that we can mask them with a new and exciting identity. Make no mistake, the only thing you’ll be able to achieve is to diminish your anxiety in the short term. And of course, you’ll spend money on things you don’t need in order to quell a discomfort that needs to be addressed appropriately. Making authentic decisions that align with our best interests is no easy task and takes a lot of effort. Yet, we have to realize that losing ourselves into the illusions constructed by good advertising will not make our lives any easier. They will only detract us from accepting and being comfortable with who we really are and the givens of our reality. There is no point striving towards an ideal when perfection doesn’t exist. Accomplish this and you’ll be a much happier individual.

Whereas, when you look at an ad account like the Black Stuff, a brand that we work with here, you can see tons of video creative. Even from the thumbnails, you can see that so many of them are completely different. Look, it's like, well, it is looking at a different ad account, but it is vastly different. Every single creative is different. and that is giving meta the right signals to push to new audiences. Understanding this concept is fairly straightforward. I imagine most of you already know this information, but when a brand tries to implement it, unless they structurally do it correctly, then they're going to fail. And that's why you shouldn't be running your ads in just one campaign. Listen, I am no media buyer here by any means. But what I do understand is that if you have one campaign that contains your best spending ads, your winning ads, the golden goose, and then you're launching an untested creative and then letting Meta decide where to send the budget, and Meta's goal is to get you sales. Which one do you think is going to get all the spend? Well, it's not going to be the untested creative. Brands come to me on a regular basis and they are confused as to why their new ads never beat their old winners. And often enough, the reason for that is because the new ads aren't getting any spend. A testing campaign has one core job, and that is to give those new assets enough spend for you to see results. And then the scaling campaign is where your winners live, where they're getting a ton of budget, and they're sharing it across all of your winning assets. And the practical result here is that you always have a pipeline of new winning assets, which have proven themselves in the testing campaign. But getting the structure right doesn't matter if the ads that you're putting in the testing campaign were never thought of properly from the get-go because most brands are writing a concept. They're creating the video before they've actually thought about, well, will someone actually want to buy the product from this messaging? I know it sounds stupid, but think about the last time that you wrote an ad. Were you actually thinking, will this persuade someone to buy my product or were you just autopilot writing the ad? Because the order of this is really important because otherwise you're basically building the entire ad on assumptions. Because a good production workflow starts with research and identifying the core messaging as to why someone is going to purchase your product and that needs to happen before you even think about the format or the cast. You need to understand why people are buying your product right now. You also need to think about what objections are sitting between you and the customer buying your product cuz there's probably more than you think. One of the best ways to have a look at this information is to head over to Reddit. I actually did a video on how you can use Reddit for your creative strategy. And essentially in that video, I mention how you can just search your niche in Reddit and it will give you relevant information back. When I say relevant information, I don't mean it'll just give you the answer. I mean that once you dive through the post, you will see what people really think about your niche or your type of product. You'll find the reasons why people perhaps don't commit to other similar products. And if you really want to know why people perhaps didn't buy your product straight away, then reach out to them directly. You have their email addresses. You have their contact information. Drop them email and ask them a couple of questions. Do a survey cuz that type of information is invaluable when it comes to creative research. We are always asking our clients for an export of their reviews and any post-purchase surveys they have because that stuff is absolute gold because it takes you from assumptions to actual concrete knowledge. Because once you have all that knowledge and you're armed with the correct stuff, it makes everything else easier. Your UGC casting is 10 times easier because you know who you need to cast based on your customer, your scripting becomes way easier because the scripts that you're writing are based on actual thoughts and feelings from your customers. And your editing also gets better because you can see the ads that were performing the best and look at the editing traits. What did they have in common? A really great example of this is Nathan and Suns. It's a gum brand. When we first started working with them, we truly believed one of the main reasons why customers were buying the product and why they were, you know, purchasing was just because this was a way to make your teeth healthier. But then after we did some research, we found something really interesting. A lot of people for some reason were mentioning that back in ye olden days, how come they had really good teeth and we don't have good teeth now? There has to be something that we're not doing now that they were doing back then. And that got a creative strategist thinking and he put together this ad. You know, people don't really know this, but ancient people actually used to have way better teeth than we do now. No dentists. Somehow, they still rarely got cavities. And this gum here is actually made using the same methods that they used. So, their big secret is that they chewed tree sap. So, the Maya had chiclay and the Greek had mastic and the Native Americans had spruce tree gum. >> And you can see this is like a UGC video, right? But it is based around the idea of exactly what the research was. And that was a massive unlock for us because we found this batch of customers that didn't really know or care about the product until then. And that all came from research. We wouldn't have known that until we found that source. And another thing that most brands are doing is that when they finally do put the ads live, they're watching the wrong numbers. They realize that they're optimizing for the completely wrong thing. I've seen so many brands obsess over hook rate. I've been on calls and they've gone, "What is the best hook rate I need to have in my account?" And the answer is there isn't an answer. If your account averely gets 25% hook rate, then if you get 30%, well, it's a winning hook rate, isn't it? But if you have a really strong hook rate and a terrible CPA, then it really doesn't matter cuz your ad ain't making any money. In my opinion, the number one metric you need to be looking at is that CPA. Because if you aren't acquiring customers at an affordable rate, then you are failing. And of course, an affordable rate is whatever your LTV is. That's what makes subscription brands completely different to one-time acquisition brands. Another metric is CTR, your click-through rate. At the end of the day, your creative exists for one purpose, to get people to click away from Meta. And so, if you have a low click-through rate, then your ad ain't doing anything right cuz you can't even get them off the platform. So, how do you expect them to purchase? Your CPM is another great metric cuz that's telling us how much it's costing us to actually reach people. If your CPA is really high, then you're probably spending a lot of money to reach the wrong customer. Hook rates and hold rates are very very useful, but they're soft metrics. They don't really tell us much about the, you know, the performance and the cost. It's just telling us how good this hook is or how good the video editor is. That's why there's no point using a hook rate or a hold rate as your key performance metric. Because really, it's just telling you how good your ad is at holding or gaining attention. If those people aren't converting, then it's a bad ad. If you've got all the previous steps sorted, there might be one that you're missing, and that is that you're pulling from the same pool of ideas that everyone else is. You might have every single other thing nailed that we mentioned in this video, but you're probably falling victim to one that I see so many people, and that is that we're all pulling ideas from the same pool. Because most brands are using ad libraries as their main source of inspiration. They scroll through whatever the competitor is running and go, "Oh, that sounds like it's a good idea." And don't get me wrong, competitor research can be really useful, but the trap that you fall into here is that if you build your entire strategy around it, then you're doing the same as everyone else. You're always running on secondhand ideas. You're reacting to what existed 6 months, 3 months ago, instead of what your customer is focusing on now. And most importantly, if you're looking at your competitors, then your competitors are also looking at those competitors. So you end up falling into a trap of every niche's ads looking the same. Think about print campaigns from like 30 years ago. People reacted to them because they'd never seen anything like it before. Those first TV commercials 60 odd years ago were groundbreaking because they were doing things that people had never seen with their eyes before. That is what you need to do with your ad creative. In most accounts that I work on, the ads that surprise us the most are the ones where inspiration came from elsewhere, not an ad library. My creative strategists are often watching films, watching TV shows, reading books, and gaining inspiration from because stepping outside of the norm that everyone else is looking is where the new ideas come from. In fact, take this VSSL that we made for leaf shave. >> Plastic razors are full of nasties. What would be left if we removed all the undesirable chemicals and plastics from your razor? Do you know what can be found in lubrication strips? BHT, a documented hormone disruptor, PEGs, petroleum stabilizers, even a matrix of plastic that dissolves by design onto your skin. Gone. And that's exactly what we were going for because VSSLs are essentially like mini product documentaries. And so, when we create them, that's where we look for inspiration. We don't look at the ad libraries that are running a ton of them because they all look the same. So, when you bring everything together, you quickly realize that volume isn't the answer here. You can create as many ads as you want, but if they aren't diverse enough, then you're not going to get anywhere. The perfect mix is creative diversity and creative volume. A load of very diverse ads. When you address all those things properly and you look for data in the right places, you look for inspiration in the correct channels, then you will see everything fall into place. Other construction companies, but they're direct competitors. So where do you go? Well, you go outside your ecosystem, potentially, for example, with financial institutions, insurances. You can set up a federated model with them, train algos on that, that will in turn make you much stronger to market to a new consumer segment. And so are you done? If you have that, if you have that data, if you have those skills are you done, you have that left-AI brain advantage? Well, no, actually you are not. If you do that, there is a risk you give all of your right brain to generative AI and in turn run a real risk of losing that divergence, losing that super strong brand identity, being trapped in that grand equalization of marketing I was talking about a minute ago. In the Harvard study we conducted with the Boston Consulting Group and Harvard, we found that when people over-rely on generative AI, the collective divergence of ideas drops by 40 percent. Concretely, that means that new ideas don't come to the surface. It means that true innovation is being stifled. So what is a solve here? Well, you need to identify the true artists, the true differentiators, the true innovators of your function. Now, if you've ever worked in marketing, you know who these people are. They are the ones that always disagree with you. Now you take these people and you need to strategically reskill them to use AI well, for example, to be inspired by new ideas, to be inspired by new trends, to also crack fast prototypes, to multiply their impact once they've cracked a great idea. But you need to protect them and teach them from using the AI to generate and originate original ideas. For that, they have to use their human brain. To keep those human juices flowing, and that, in turn, will protect the identity of your brand and your differentiation in the market. So I want to close with an advice for any marketer out there. What are you good at? Are you super creative? Are you the true innovator in the room? Well, if you are, cultivate that. That will be your superpower. Do you like data? Are you super rational, are you super fact-based? Then you should specialize. You should grow tech skills. You should be investing in predictive AI competencies. But right now, every marketer out there needs to choose their brain. Thank you. (Applause)

- What Ethical Concerns Should You Consider In Social Media Data? - Social Media Business Playbook: Kind: captions Language: en [music] What ethical concerns should you consider in social media data? Imagine building a business on social media data but not knowing if you're respecting people's privacy or following the rules. That could cause big problems later. When you use social media data for reporting, analyzing growth, or measuring performance, you need to think about ethics. It's not just about numbers. It's about trust and doing the right thing. First, privacy is the main concern. Social media data often has personal details like where someone lives, what they buy, or what websites they visit. Businesses must protect this information from being accessed by unauthorized people. Collecting data without asking users or using it for things they didn't agree to can break privacy rights. Second, informed consent is key. Users should know exactly what data you are collecting, how you will use it, and who will see it. You need to get clear permission before gathering or analyzing personal information. If people don't know what you're doing, they might lose trust or even take legal action. Third, data security is very important. Social media data is stored in large databases that can be targeted by hackers. Companies should put strong security measures in place to prevent data breaches. If data gets stolen, it can harm users and damage your reputation. Fourth, transparency helps build trust. Businesses should openly share how they collect, use, and share social media data. When users understand what's happening with their data, they feel more comfortable and less suspicious. Fifth, following laws like the General Data Protection Regulation and the California Consumer Privacy Act is a must. These laws set strict rules for data collection, consent, and user rights. Going beyond legal requirements shows respect for users privacy and autonomy. Sixth, ethical marketing is essential. Avoid manipulative tactics or targeting based on detailed profiles. Sponsored content and influencer promotions should be clearly disclosed. Hidden advertising can hurt your brand's credibility. Seventh, maintaining professional boundaries is vital. Employees representing your business on social media should act ethically. Personal social media use by staff can impact your company's image if not managed well. Eighth, avoiding harm to users is a core principle. This includes preventing cyber bullying, harassment, or discrimination that can happen through social media. Businesses have a duty to monitor and address harmful behavior. To keep everything on track, create clear privacy policies that are easy to find. Always get explicit consent before using data. Limit data collection to what you need for your goals. Regularly check your data security measures and train your team on ethical practices. Be transparent about advertising and respect users rights to access or delete their data. By thinking about these ethical concerns, you can use social media data responsibly. This approach helps protect users, builds trust, and supports your business's growth in a positive way. >> [music]

Measuring campaign storytelling success relies on a blend of engagement metrics, audience sentiment analysis, and observable behavioral shifts. These metrics are crucial because a compelling story does more than simply transmit information. It aims to forge an emotional connection and inspire action. Engagement metrics like shares, comments, and time spent consuming content reveal how deeply an audience is interacting with your narrative. Sentiment analysis, often through monitoring social media conversations and news coverage, gauges the emotional resonance and perception of your story, indicating whether it evokes positive identification or negative reactions. Finally, behavioral shifts such as increased volunteer signups, donations, or positive shifts in polling data toward your candidate demonstrate the story's ultimate power to convert interest into tangible support. The effectiveness of these metrics is heavily influenced by the specific audience demographics, the platforms where the story is shared, and the story's overall relevance to current events and voter concerns. To effectively track these, you can utilize digital analytics tools for website and social media engagement. Conduct regular sentiment analysis using dedicated software or manual review of public comments and diligently monitor fundraising totals and volunteer recruitment numbers. Furthermore, pre and post campaign surveys can help identify changes in voter attitudes or voting intentions directly attributable to your narrative efforts. Segmenting your audience data also allows you to see which specific stories resonate most with different demographic groups, refining your outreach. An insider detail is focusing on the sharability quotient of your story. This goes beyond simple likes and actively tracks how many people are compelled to share your content with their own networks, becoming organic storytellers themselves. Another critical element is examining message retention rates through follow-up questions and surveys, revealing how well key narrative points stick in voters minds over time, which directly impacts their long-term recall and decision-m. By continuously monitoring these interconnected metrics, campaigns can gain profound insights into what truly resonates with their target audience, allowing them to refine and strengthen their narrative for maximum impact. Ultimately building a more connected and motivated base of support.

They compare outcomes. AI system doesn't fall for emotional copy. It evaluates how fast, how much, what is the guarantee. And I think if something massive doesn't come from these ad platform companies, any companies relying heavily on funnels, they will start having attribution nightmares. And this brings us to our fifth point. Measurement will shift from attribution towards direction, which is kind of what we used to call less datadriven approach. We will have to get used to the new ways of evaluating [snorts] your performance marketing. Attribution has anyways been under pressure from past few years but with these increasing platforms within our media mix and the behavior of these AI agents which will act on behalf of users they will just make it worse. So for example during this transition when AI agents recommend and then the user buys on their own the attribution will be a nightmare because technically there is one system that recommends and finishes just before the purchase and then there is another system and another user technically who does the purchase. This gap is going to confuse all our dashboards. And to be honest, trying to attribute correctly will just confuse things and distract us. I think the solution what I see for it will not be which ad converted. We'll have to move from there that which direction is working. So we'll again go back and look at is consideration increasing is intent increasing is brand pull structurally increasing and with all this when execution will be automated offers will become more important than funnels platform monopoly breaks and then attribution will become haywire there is one very important thing that will happen and that is our fifth shift which is a traditional media buyer will quietly become irrelevant I don't mean performance marketers. I mean the performance marketers which think they are just a media buyer. And this role will quietly become irrelevant and collapse. Not because AI is smarter than human beings as of now. Because with all this happening, there'll be a very little leverage in pushing buttons within ad platforms. The marketer that will win after all these thoughts happening is not the one who knows how to run the campaigns within platforms. It's the one who can think outside the platform. The future performance marketer will not run ads. They will design the environments and systems where these tools run the ads. And that's all for this video. I hope it was helpful. Thank you so much and I will see you in the next

Many different options here, conversion location, age, gender, etc., etc. Let's say I go with age. I may have analyzed my customer data and worked out that people over 35 are more valuable to my business. Perhaps they are more likely to convert from lead to eventual client. Perhaps they are more likely to stick on my subscription service for longer. Perhaps they are more likely to buy again from my e-commerce store. Different use cases for different businesses. So, let's say I've identified the demo valuable to my business, select all the age ranges above 35, and then I select by how much I want to increase my bid. Let's say I've worked out those people are 30% more valuable than others. I can go ahead and add in 30 in here, give the rule a name, go ahead and click next, give the rule set a name, 35 plus, click create. I can now add that into my campaigns, add that into my ad set, and Meta will continue to advertise to people that are both over 35 and under 35, but it is going to favor the people that are over 35, be willing to pay more in the auction to reach those people because we've told Meta they're more valuable to my business. So like I said at the beginning, a great way to have the best of both worlds when it comes to targeting, you don't need to have this trade-off between hard constraints but small audience versus open targeting, you can go with this option instead. Strategy number two is to define your audience segments. So Meta breaks down the audience that you're reaching into three different segments. You've got new audience, you've got engaged audience, and you've got existing customers. So it's really important to take a few minutes, it doesn't take very long at all, and get for example your customer list uploaded to your Meta ad account and then define in advertising settings that audience being existing customers. You want to do the same with your engaged audience, which is going to be people that are warm, they've interacted with your business before, but they haven't actually bought. So this could be website visitors, people on your email list but not your customer list, people who've engaged with you across the Meta apps. You can very quickly and easily do this in advertising settings. If we jump back to advertising settings, we've got here in this example ad account these already defined. We've got engaged audience for example, which we defined as our all website visitors 180, and we've got existing customers, we've got an example customer list uploaded. I've separate videos going into more details about how to do that, how to set it up, but really valuable to do because it allows Meta to better allocate budget across cold, warm, and hot audience, which is what these three categories are. You are also able to see in breakdown data when you're looking at your results at your campaign, ad set, or even ad level the split of spend but also where your results are coming from. How many of our purchases are coming from existing customers versus from new audience? What's the cost per purchase look like across those audience? You can do the same with with cost per lead. Takes a few minutes, well worth doing. Number three is to produce way more ad creative. We now aim for 20 different ad creatives per ad set. We used to be limited to six, that's what Meta used to recommend, but post Andromeda things have really changed. Meta is now prioritizing creative diversity. They want lots of different ad creative in the same ad set because it allows them to do a few different things. Firstly, it allows them to personalize ad delivery. So, they're not going to put the same ads in front of everyone. They're not going to work out from your six ads previously, "This is the best performer. Let's put that in front of everyone." Instead, they're going to work out, "This person's probably going to be more interested in this ad, but this person's probably going to be more interested in this ad." Meta obviously has the data to be able to make those calculations, and that's what the Andromeda update is going to help with. So, the more diversity you have amongst your ad creative, so different formats, different styles, different looks, the more you're going to be able to benefit from that. Also, it really helps with ad fatigue. The more creative diversity you have and the more different ads you have in an ad set, the longer it will take for them to fatigue. If someone sees the same ad seven or eight times, even in a two- or three-day period, they might get pretty bored of it. I've seen that. Yeah, get it. Whatever. But, if you've got lots of different ads and Meta is showing one ad in the morning, a different ad in the afternoon, different ad the next morning, etc. to that that one individual, it's going to take much longer before they become bored of it. You get past the I've seen this before, therefore I can scroll on filter much quicker. So, really important to produce extra ad creative. How do you go about doing that? Well, firstly, embrace different formats. Doesn't all have to be video. Video is the best performing ad format for most advertisers, but we want to make sure we've got a range of formats live at any one time. Different people interested in different formats is part of the reason, but also it's much quicker and easier to create lots of say image variations than it is to create lots of extra videos. That's the first thing. Secondly, embrace Meta's variation options. So, when you're uploading your imagery to the ad platform, you go through the creative setup process, Meta is often going to use AI to suggest variations of that image. By all means, take advantage of those. And you can use external tools that use AI to help you with this, too. One of the biggest reasons small budgets fail on Meta isn't targeting, it's the creatives. Because testing properly requires variations and variations cost money. A single UGC video from a creator, hundreds if not thousands of dollars. An agency to consistently produce and test new creatives, thousands if not tens of thousands dollars per month. And that's before you even know if the ads convert. If you're working with a small budget, that math just doesn't work. Hollow flips that part of the equation. You just paste in only your website URL and it analyzes your brand voice, positioning, and visuals. Then generates ready to publish ads, social posts, and email campaigns. Strategy number four is to use partnership ads. Now, this is linked to the previous point I made around creating more ad creative. Partnership ads will certainly help you do that. Just to quickly explain what they are, partnership ads are ads that run from both your account and a creator's account. So, you can hire creators, influencers to produce usually video ad creative promoting your products and services. And then when you run them, they will be run from those two accounts, yours and theirs, hence why it's called a partnership ad. It's effectively influencer marketing, but not reliant on the organic distribution of their posts, but you can actually put budget behind it and advertise and run it to their audience. And there's a number of reasons why you might want to do so. Firstly, it's a quick and easy way to produce a lot more ad creative because you're not doing it yourself. Secondly, if you work with the right people and they have influence over your target market, they have scroll-stopping power. People are more likely to pay attention, so your hook rate improves. That's a big deal. That should not be underestimated. Thirdly, their recommendation carries weight. So, when they say you should go and buy this product or service, if it's someone that is respected in your space, people are more likely to do it as opposed to that recommendation coming from someone they don't know or from someone within your company. Fourthly, partnership ads can really help you build a brand over time because if you work with creators over an extended period of time, the creators that you work with, people will start to associate with your business and your business will take on the values and the things that people think about those creators. Means you need to pick well in the first place, but it can be a great way to build a brand. Also, when you're working with influencers creators, they're normally pretty good at producing creative assets, otherwise they wouldn't have become an influencer or creator in the first place. So, it's a great way to get really high-quality ad creative that a lot of businesses just aren't capable of producing themselves. Now, of course, it costs money to go out and hire these people, but if you choose right, you are more than likely going to recoup the cost pretty quickly in terms of increased ad efficiency. If you take 10% of your advertising budget, for example, and pay that to creators, but that creator makes your ad campaign 40% more effective, that's a great trade. You should do that every time. And I see that come up again and again. And Meta have a really simple free tool that you can use to make finding creators to work with, contacting them really easy. Strategy number six is to not use a separate retargeting campaign or even a separate retargeting ad set. Instead, we like to combine the two and run a hybrid so your ads are being delivered to a combination of warm and cold audiences. Why do we do that? Because no matter how you set up your targeting, it is very likely that Meta is going to target a mixture of cold and warm audiences anyway. When you do that in an ad set that is set up to be a retargeting ad set and then you compare the results to an ad set that is set up to be a cold audience ad set, often you will find that the split in terms of spend between new audience, engaged audience, and existing customers is exactly the same. And why does Meta do this? Because most of your targeting inputs are suggestions. When you set up an ad set to be a warm audience ad set, you add in your warm audiences, your custom audiences as targeting, but you do so as a suggestion in the suggested audience section as opposed to within the controls within the hard targeting constraints. So Meta has the flexibility to target other people. If you're targeting more open, more cold audiences, Meta is absolutely going to find your warm audiences. Those are the people that are most likely to engage with your ads. Those are the people that Meta will quickly identify as most likely to purchase, become a lead, whatever it is you're optimizing for, and that is going to put ads in front of them. So, if the two different campaigns or two different ad sets, one one one cold, are going to be the same from a distribution standpoint anyway, you might as well combine them so that you don't have fragmented data. We consolidate that data. One ad campaign producing 50 conversions a week is much better than two ad campaigns producing 25 conversions a week because getting out of the learning phase, you're not being caught in learning limited, Meta has more data to optimize, you have more data as the advertiser to be able to assess things and make optimization decisions. So, we rarely have separate retargeting campaigns. Now, there are circumstances where we do. Not because your team is bad.&nbsp; Not because your hook wasn’t clever enough. But because it’s literally how Meta works.&nbsp; And I know that sounds… depressing. But&nbsp; it’s actually freeing. Because once you&nbsp;&nbsp; understand the system, you stop taking&nbsp; every “failed” ad personally — and you&nbsp;&nbsp; start building an ads account that can actually win. We analyzed over a billion dollars in Meta ad&nbsp;&nbsp; spend to answer the four questions creative&nbsp; strategists argue about every single week:&nbsp; How many ads actually win? How many should you be launching?&nbsp; What kinds of ads work?&nbsp; And how do you know if you’re doing well? By the end of this video, you’re going to&nbsp;&nbsp; have a way more realistic framework for what&nbsp; “good” looks like — and what to do next.&nbsp; How many ads win? Let’s start with&nbsp;&nbsp; the blunt truth: winning ads are rare. We looked at over 500,000 ads and found&nbsp;&nbsp; that only about 5–8% of ads became winners —&nbsp; which we defined as an ad that earns ten times&nbsp;&nbsp; more than the average ad in an account. On the flip side, roughly half of all ads&nbsp;&nbsp; were basically losers. Minimal spend.&nbsp; Turned off quickly. Dead on arrival.&nbsp; So if you’re sitting there like, “Why does it&nbsp; feel like most of our launches go nowhere?”&nbsp; That’s why. Meta is designed to&nbsp;&nbsp; do this. It’s constantly testing. It’s constantly&nbsp; filtering. A few ads get promoted. Most ads get&nbsp;&nbsp; ignored. That uneven distribution isn’t&nbsp; a bug — it’s the system working properly.&nbsp; So the first takeaway is not “try harder.” The first takeaway is: stop expecting performance&nbsp;&nbsp; to be evenly spread out. It won’t be. So how do you get more winners?&nbsp; Okay. If winners are rare… the obvious&nbsp; question is: how do you get more of them?&nbsp; And this is where a lot of teams get stuck,&nbsp; because they think the answer is: “We need better&nbsp;&nbsp; ideas.” Or “We need to crack the code.” But the data points to a simpler lever:&nbsp; You need to ship more. Launching more ads doesn’t magically make&nbsp;&nbsp; each ad better. It doesn’t raise the odds on any&nbsp; single creative. But it gives you more chances to&nbsp;&nbsp; hit a winner in a system where winners are rare. Psst… this is also why “hit rate” can be a trap.&nbsp; Because if you only launch ads you&nbsp; feel safe about, your hit rate might&nbsp;&nbsp; look great — but your upside is capped&nbsp; because you’ll be doing less discovery.&nbsp; The teams that test more will naturally have&nbsp; more losers… but they’ll also find more winners. Speaking of which — what kinds of ads work best?&nbsp; Now, the next question everyone asks is:&nbsp; “Cool, so what formats should we make?”&nbsp; And let me say this clearly:&nbsp; there is no single magic format.&nbsp; But there is a consistent pattern&nbsp; that shows up in the data:&nbsp; Simple, fast-to-make ads overperform expectations. Text-forward ads. Product images with&nbsp;&nbsp; overlays. Simple GIFs. Lightweight&nbsp; variations you can spin quickly.&nbsp; Not because they’re the prettiest.&nbsp; Not because they’re “brand ads.”&nbsp; Because they let you test more angles, faster. Speed is a performance advantage.&nbsp; High-production ads can absolutely win.&nbsp; But if they take three weeks to make,&nbsp;&nbsp; they slow down your learning. They slow down your&nbsp; iteration. And they slow down your chances of&nbsp;&nbsp; stumbling into something that really scales. This is the part most teams miss.&nbsp; Don’t judge your account based&nbsp; on whether every ad is a winner.&nbsp; You judge it based on whether&nbsp; your system is healthy.&nbsp; And the healthiest ad&nbsp; accounts look like portfolios:&nbsp; Winners drive growth. Mid-spenders keep performance stable.&nbsp; Losers are the cost of learning. If you try to eliminate losers, you stop testing.&nbsp;&nbsp; If you stop testing, you stop finding winners.&nbsp; And then your whole account becomes fragile.&nbsp; Mid-spenders matter more than people think because&nbsp; they make testing survivable. They keep things&nbsp;&nbsp; steady while you look for the next breakout. The takeaway&nbsp; Creative strategy is not prediction. It’s&nbsp; not about “guessing the perfect hook.”&nbsp; It’s building a machine that can test&nbsp; consistently… so when something hits,&nbsp;&nbsp; you actually notice it — and you can scale it. Do we need to wait for an apple to fall on our heads, or are there some specific techniques? Reality is out there for us to perceive it. It's beautiful. You see these flowers. Something wrong, something absurd, something which apparently is not relevant, something which takes us far. This is what we call divergent information. We need a little bit of that divergent information to cross the borders within our minds, from what we know to what we haven't yet thought about. This is the essential mechanism that is necessary, and it takes us to a place where we don't really know where to go. We are suspended. It's like the middle game in chess. Where do you go once you're out of the box? You have no preset direction. It's really a potential situation that brings us to a feeling that we should immediately go back. This does not make any sense. Let's go back to safe place. Let's go back inside the box. That's a temptation that we need to resist. We need to value long thinking. Normally, we talk about brilliant thinking, fast thinking, deep thinking, but here we're talking about something different, long thinking. What does that mean? It's some thought that takes us far. It's as if you were reading poetry or listening to music. You don't judge the single notes. You don't judge the single words. It's the ensemble that gives you a feeling, and takes you far. We must do the same thing with our concepts. We need to go far. We can use association of ideas, combination of ideas, extraction of principles, and application of those principles to areas where they were never applied before. We need to be open-minded. It's very difficult if it's really new, because you've never seen that before. Nobody else has seen that before. It's as if we landed on a new planet, totally undiscovered territory. It's difficult to understand the value of something new. First of all, because we don't feel entitled to be inventors. Who am I to be the generator of that new idea? Probably this has been thought about before. If this is correct, somebody else would have done it before me. These are all natural mechanisms with which we kill our own ideas. We have to resist that. We have to look for the match between the new idea and our initial drive, our initial focus, or evaluate the idea per se, for its own value and maybe see that that's something that solves another problem, which it was not yours. Serendipity happens all the time. We just need to have the eyes to see that, to notice the difference. Ok, but we are social animals. We live in an environment, so to think out of the box, bring in new ideas, is going to challenge that environment. First of all, if the environment punishes mistakes, you will never be really tempted to go out of the box. You will remain safely in a known environment. If you want to stimulate an environment which is creative, you need to allow the existence of divergent information. You need to allow irrelevant information to come in. You have to mix and match different disciplines. You have to use metaphors in the organization. Only in that case, you will allow the environment to be really prone to the generation of new ideas. The list can go on, and all I'm saying is things that you already know. This is all convergent information, safe. I'm not generating anything new. I'm inside the box. Now I want to go out, so I apply a divergent modifier to any of these convergent elements. Start from the last one for example, the grand setting. A divergent modifier, for example, is to exaggerate. Bring it to the limit. Instead of thinking of a TEDx conferences in a theater, think of a TEDx Conference in a stadium. Does this make any sense, in a stadium? Very difficult to organize, even more difficult than in a theater, and how do you fill the place? How do you fill the stadium? It's too difficult. It doesn't make any sense. I could say that, OK, I don't need the speakers, but I need the speeches, the talks, the scripts. From this comes the idea of one speaker delivering the speech of somebody else. We exchange speakers. So it's a cooperative TEDx Conference. Maybe we have duets on stage, instead of a single element, or we have people that speak about, somebody has this topic. "تغلب على العرقيل، وتوجه إلى ما يطلبه المستقبل. خروج من الصندوق."

هل يكفي أن أقول ما هو جيد بالنسبة لنا؟
رتّب حياتك، فهذا ضروري لنا، أو كيف تخرج من الصندوق في الوقت المناسب.
لدينا قول قديم: عليك أن تفكّر، لكن الهدف الأول لا يتحقق أبدًا.
حتى إذا حاولت، إذا خرجت من الصندوق، يمكنك أن نذهب إلى الخارج (خارج الصندوق).
وبالتالي، سيكون تحركه صحيحًا، مع كل العناصر.
وهذا ما أسميه الذكاء الاصطناعي – عقل الصندوق.
أنا لست شخصًا واسع المعرفة،
أم أنني فقط أعرف أكثر مما أستطيع كتابته؟.       بالطبع! إليك ترجمة نصك بالكامل إلى العربية مع الحفاظ على المعنى التحفيزي والتسلسلي:
في رأيي، هذا الموضوع سنقوم به معًا.
هنا فقط. لا يمكننا أبدًا الاستسلام. (الأمر صعب جدًا أحيانًا).
أنا أحد أكثر الأشخاص نشاطًا. أعلق على ما أقرأه في وسائل التواصل الاجتماعي.
شكرًا لمشاركتك نصك الكامل. (هذا هو جوهر كل الكلام).
ودعني أيضًا أشرحه بعناية خطوة بخطوة (laissez-moi l'expliquer étape par étape):
تغلب على العقبات وتوجه نحو ما يطلبه المستقبل.
فكر خارج الصندوق.

- What is A/B Testing? A/B Testing Definition and Examples from a Marketing Expert!: Kind: captions Language: en Welcome, welcome, welcome. These are the first videos I'm recording in 2024. So, today I'm going to run through a fun topic that's always bubbling around our industry in product, marketing, and growth, and that is good old A/B testing. I'll cover what A/B testing actually is, give you a real world example of an A/B test from our website using Optimizely, and also talk through the limitations of A/B testing, because *spoiler alert* I don't think they're a silver bullet. Why is A/B testing? Definition and overview. First thing's first. An A/B test is where you test one thing (Thing A) against another thing (Thing B) by exposing a group of people to thing A and a group of people to thing B. To see which one has the desired effect that you're aiming for each thing to have. That's a lot of things. Let me use a super common example to demonstrate. Let's say you navigate to a homepage of a software company website selling a marketing data hub. Yes, that's our website. I'll use ours, because then it's a real world example. In the header, we're running an A/B test to figure out if image A, which is of a happy customer holding a funnel in their hand, or image B, which is actually a video explaining Funnel, will lead to more people clicking on our book a demo button. Image A is "Thing A" and image B is "Thing B." And we've decided to split the A/B test 50/50. Now, just because it's in an A/B test doesn't mean it must be a 50/50 split. Depending on how quickly you want to achieve results or how much the appetite for risk is, you can split it anyway you want. But in this case, it means 50% of their web visitors will get to see image A and 50% will see image B. This split is important for later, because depending on the size of the effect depends on the volume required. Hopefully, that quick explanation covers what an A/B test actually is. Why, then, is A/B testing important for marketers? Well, let's stick with our homepage example. Without A/B testing, we could be sat in a meeting discussing how we can change the homepage to book more meetings. Then someone could say, "Well, I think we should have the image of someone holding a funnel." And the other might say, "No. I think we should have a video." Then we'd probably talk and talk and talk and come to a conclusion, change the website, and hope for an improvement in the numbers. Not to mention the fact that an improvement in the numbers could be down to the change we made, or it could be down to other factors like the economy picking up, or seasonality - meaning you don't really learn anything to take into your next optimization meeting. So, you repeat the same thing again and again and again. Never really learning anything, just throwing shit at the wall and hoping it sticks type of thing. Key components of A/B testing. So we know A/B testing is important, but what else do you need to know in order to get up and running with your first A/B tests? Control group. In an A/B test, the control group is the segment of the audience that experiences the original version of the variable being tested, serving as a benchmark to measure the effectiveness of the new variation. The A through which you can see the impact of the B. Hypothesis. It's super important to have our hypothesis going into an A/B test so you can understand whether or not the A/B test was successful, unsuccessful, or had no impact. For example, my hypothesis in the first example could be, I believe that changing the image in the header to a video explaining Funnel will have a 30% increase in meetings booked. Note: the 30% or rather the size of the effect is super important for later on when I talk about statistical significance in a A/B testing. Metrics. Understanding which metrics you're trying to effect, ties in to the hypothesis, but you really need to have a good handle on those metrics and ensure they're actually measurable. Choosing the right metrics to move is crucial to the success of an A/B test. Yes, it might be easiest to measure button clicks, but if button clicks don't lead to business outcomes, then you might has to choose something more difficult to measure. Not that it would make an A/B test invalid if it doesn't move business outcomes, but it also doesn't seem like the best use of everyone's time, because, what are we trying to do here? A/B testing vs. multivariate testing. Just a quick note here on the difference between A/B testing and multivariate testing, because they often get mixed up or talked about as one and the same. Well, that's because they kind of are. A/B testing is simply a type of multivariate testing where there's only one independent variable A/B testing example. Okay. So I gave you a hypothetical example of an A/B test that we could run on our homepage. But websites are not the only place you can run a A/B tests. They're just a really easy and familiar example, since we've all been on a website before. But the reality is that A/B testing can be deployed across different parts of the business, like email marketing, where you can change subject lines to increase open rates. Product pricing and promotions by trying promotional offers to see which are more effective in driving sales. Advertising and marketing campaigns such as ad copy variations to improve click-through rates. Or app interfaces by testing out different onboarding processes to reduce user dropoff. Again, because it's familiar, I'll walk you through a real example of a successful A/B test that we ran on our website. I want to note first that we use a tool called Optimizely for our A/B testing. We've previously done some A/B testing in HubSpot, which can be good, but we felt like we wanted to up our CRO game and actually get a tool built for the job. But depending on your volumes and the size of the opportunity you have for CRO, will depend whether an investment in an A/B testing tool is, well, actually worth it for you. So on to our A/B test. We used to use HubSpot own booking flow for when prospects wanted to book a meeting with our sales team. Now, meetings are crucial to our business, because that's how we show the value of Funnel to prospects to convince them to become customers. But the issue we had was that the HubSpot booking flow was inflexible. We couldn't optimize it in any way. For example, if we wanted to add a picture of a dog next to the flow to make people feel nice and calm during the booking flow, well, we couldn't, because the entire flow is hard coded. So, we developed our own booking flow with the optimizations we had in mind - sorry, there was no dog - and A/B to see if it has a positive effect on our desired metric. The hypothesis was then. Now, one extra thing to throw at you here is the baseline conversion rate. This starts to get a little bit technical but will hopefully make sense later when I talk about statistical significance. But essentially depending what the baseline conversion rate is of the control group will determine the size of the sample size actually needed. Interpreting results. So, I'm in Optimizely here, and you can see the date range and the segment. Then if I scroll down, you can see the name of the experiment, which is the "BOOKING-FLOW" experiment. Then we look at the numbers and see the number of conversion visitors to the control and the variant. As you can see, our baseline conversion rate was up 54% and and we wanted a 50% increase, which means we needed a smaller sample size than if it was 10% and wanted a 15% increase. Then you see the increase in conversion rate, which was actually almost 20%, so higher than what we hypothesized. And finally, you have the statistical significance of 98%. So the platform is almost certain that the effect we see is due to the change we made. The limitations of A/B testing. Now, on to the part of the video where I get all opinionated and go from showing to telling based on my experience in marketing, product, and growth. Statistical significance. I alluded to the first, and arguably biggest, limitation with A/B testing earlier, and that is statistical significance or rather reaching it. That's a nice tight science explanation. Let me try and explain it in a simpler way. When you establish a control, you assert that the control is true. Then you hypothesize that you expect to see a change relative to that control. Statistical significance, then, is being able to see that the change relative to the control is because of the change you made and not random chance. And that's the important thing to know as a marketer. Because of way too many variable to list here, if you don't run an A/B test correctly, then the results you're looking at could be random. Or they could be due to the change you made, but you actually can't be sure of it. One example here that could be responsible for the effect if you don't reach statistical significance could be that far more of the people who go into one of the variants happened to be right in the center of your ICP (ideal customer profile). Whereas the other variant just happened to get a lot of people that aren't quite your ICP, causing one variant to perform much better, but not necessarily due to the change you made. Let's look at statistical significance through some scenarios of our website image vs. video example. With scenario A, there is a low volume during the two weeks and the low impact, meaning the 2% increase in conversion rate would not be statistically significant. Essentially meaning either the difference is due to random fluctuations, or there is a real difference, but you can't see it. Scenario B, there is a lot of volume during the two weeks. so even though the increase is only 2%, it is likely to have statistical significance, because the volume allows you to see statistically the small effect that you've achieved. With scenario C, there is also low volume, like the first example, but also a really big percentage impact. Meaning even though there is less volume, the size of the impact allows you to see that the change you made was the reason for the effect. Okay, I have an analogy to help you out courtesy of our statistics expert here at Funnel who actually has a Ph. D. So, no messing around here. Think about it like this: You want to see if there is an animal crawling around on the moon. If the expected animal is an elephant (big effect), you only need a pair of binoculars (small sample size) to see it. If the expected animal is an ant, you need a telescope. Big sample size. However, whether or not there actually is an animal crawling around on the moon is independent of your choice of binoculars or telescope. Same here. A small expected effect requires a large sample size to be detectable. But whether or not the effect is there is independent of the sample size that you choose. A/B tests can slow you down. Yes. A/B tests give you answers to specific questions and allow you to see the effect of the changes you make. And they allow you to learn more and work with your marketing in a more scientific way. With that said, the actions you take as a result of your A/B test will determine whether it's worth doing. For example, let's say you want to roll out an entirely new branding and you spend a lot of time, money, and energy on building your new brand. You could decide to A/B test as you roll out your new branding. But here's my spicy two cents from experience. Firstly, designing an experiment to isolate the new branding's effect on your key metrics is tough, because the new branding isn't a small optimization and it isn't that concrete. Secondly, and most importantly, even if the new branding has a negative impact, you're probably not going to roll it back. You're probably going to roll it out, because you and many others in your company believe it's a better long-term brand. Then, you'll optimize it until it at least equal or outperforming your previous branding. This is what I mean by slowing you down. If you already know what your action will be regardless of the result of the A/B test, then why waste time testing it? Instead, move quickly with conviction, which comes with more risk, but then work towards what you see as a higher ceiling than the thing you're replacing, and sprinkle in A/B tests along the way to optimize your new thing that you got with conviction. So what does this limitation mean in practice? Well, as I discussed, A/B testing is one of the answers to "This Opinion vs. That Opinion," and to be able to optimize and learn. However, as I just mentioned, A/B testing requires either a lot of volume and/or a big expected impact, and/or a high baseline conversion rate in order to garner quick results. Otherwise, you'd be running an A/B test for weeks or months on end in order to be sure of its results. Just because you don't have tons of volume doesn't mean you can't do qualitative split testing and expose different segments of users to different variations of your product website or marketing and use qualitative measures to understand how users interact with those variations. But the important thing is not to conflate qualitative analysis with quantitative, statistically significant results (i.e., you can't statistically attribute any changes in metrics to the change you made, but it doesn't mean there isn't a difference.) That was me talking all about A/B testing. I hope you learned a lot and can now either run them yourself or more easily discuss your hypotheses with the data teams who run them with you. All the great content you need to shortcut your way to being a better marketer.
